(i) W has 3 valence electrons → W3+; Y has 5 → gains 3 → Y3−. Formula W3+Y3− (WY).

(ii) X (4 valence e−, like C) and Z (6, like O): XZ2 (accept XZ).

4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3

  • The bonding is ionic (Al3+ and O2−) in a giant lattice.
  • The melting point is high because of the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
  • It conducts when molten because the ions are then free to move.

(i) Na+ is smaller than K+ (same charge), so it has a higher charge density and attracts F− more strongly.

(ii) Ca2+ has a larger charge (and is smaller) than K+. Its greater charge density gives stronger electrostatic attraction between the ions.

Ionic: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (cations and anions) in a lattice.

Metallic: electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) and a sea of delocalized electrons.

Saying only "metal + non-metal" does not describe the bonding and scores no mark.
Lattice enthalpy decreases from LiCl to RbCl: the cation radius increases down the group, so the distance between ion centres increases and the electrostatic attraction between the ions is weaker.
Mg2+ has a higher charge (2+ vs 1+) and a smaller radius than Na+, so its attraction to Cl− ions is much stronger.

(i) Ions: Ca2+ and NO3−. Force: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. ("Ionic" alone is not accepted.)

(ii) The N and O atoms within the nitrate ion are covalently bonded.
Most → least endothermic: MgF2 > MgCl2 > CaCl2. F− is smaller than Cl−, and Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+; smaller ions are closer together, so electrostatic attraction (lattice enthalpy) is greater.

(i) Any two: Mg loses two electrons to O (Mg2+ and O2− formed); ions are arranged in a 3D lattice; held by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

(ii) The electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the two bonded atoms.

(iii) The electronegativity difference between Mg and O is large (ionic, > ~1.8), whereas between C and O it is smaller (covalent).

(i) Na₂O is ionic: a giant lattice held by strong electrostatic attraction between ions. P₄O₁₀ is covalent with a simple molecular structure: only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to melt it, so its melting point is lower.

(ii) P₄O₁₀: solid no, molten no (no ions). Na₂O: solid no (ions fixed), molten yes (mobile ions).

(i) Chromium(III) oxide. The (III) is needed.

(ii) Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, Cr³⁺ and O²⁻. The ions form by electron transfer from Cr atoms to O atoms.

(iii) In the solid the ions are held in a rigid lattice and are not free to move.

(i) Liquid MgCl₂ conducts and liquid PCl₃ does not. MgCl₂ is ionic, so its ions are free to move when molten. PCl₃ is covalent (molecular), so it has no charged particles. All three points for only one substance scores [1].

(ii) MgCl₂: pH about 4 to less than 7 (slightly acidic). The small, highly charged Mg²⁺ ion polarizes the water in [Mg(H₂O)₆]²⁺, which releases H⁺ (hydrolysis).
PCl₃: pH about 0–4. It reacts with water to form HCl and H₃PO₃ (not H₃PO₄).
Mg3N2 (magnesium nitride) – Mg also reacts with the N2 in air. (MgCO3, Mg(OH)2 etc. were also accepted.)

A giant 3-D lattice with a regularly repeating arrangement of Mg2+ and O2− ions, held by electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions (ionic bonding). Writing just “ionic” is not enough.
Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (here Ca2+ and C22−) in a lattice.
A giant, 3-D regularly repeating lattice of ions (Na+ and O2−), held by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (ionic bonding). Just “ionic” without description is not enough.
Ba2+ and Mg2+ have the same charge, but Ba2+ has a much larger ionic radius. The ions are further apart, so the electrostatic attraction is weaker and less energy is needed to separate the lattice.
